title: Instance Masks from Shared Features
summary: How Mirage combines shared mask prototypes with local coefficients, and why the CPU only needs a small feature patch for each object.
body_markdown:
A box around a stop sign also catches some of the trees and sky behind it. If you're building an app that selects the sign, those extra pixels matter. The pole is a little harder still. It is thin, partly hidden by the sign, and its outline changes along its length. We need a mask to describe which pixels belong to each object.


In Mirage, we build these masks from the image features already used for detection. We compute 32 spatial maps that all objects can share, then give each object 32 coefficients to combine them. That lets us reuse most of the spatial work. On the CPU, we go a step further and compute an object's coefficients from just a 5×55\\times5

The shared-prototype construction comes from[YOLACT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.02689) . We'll follow it from image features to an outline, then look at why such a small patch is enough for the coefficients. Along the way, the geometry helps explain both what sharing saves and what it asks the model to give up.

The artificial patch boundary is too far away to affect the central output through two layers. This is the reason we can replace the full-grid calculation with a local one. It relies on every operation having the locality described above. Adding global pooling, attention or a normalisation over the whole grid would change the dependency picture.


We checked this with synthetic 128-channel features, including centres near image and padding edges where mistakes are easy to miss. The patch and full-grid outputs agreed to floating-point precision. That gives us a check of the local computation; judging the masks themselves still needs images and reference masks.

That is about **160.4 million** multiply-accumulates for the dense map versus **0.98 million per requested object** for the patch implementation. Several objects may repeat work on overlapping patches. These are operation counts for the coefficient branch, not whole-model speedups.


The prototype maps are computed on the first mask request and reused for the remaining objects in that image. Their FP32 cache occupies **2 MiB** . Avoiding the dense coefficient map saves another **0.5 MiB** of output storage, although patch intermediates still need memory. Image features, prototype computation, mask assembly and output conversion remain part of the cost.


## From a probability field to an outline


Once we have a probability field, we still need to decide what to give the application. An outline is convenient for drawing over a camera view. A bitmap is more useful when you need to select or count individual pixels. You can choose the representation in the same call that describes the objects.


```text
import   cactus


vision   =   cactus.Mirage()
result   =   vision.describe(
"photo.jpg"  ,
sections  =  [  "objects"  ],
fields  =  [  "bbox"  ,   "score"  ,   "mask"  ],
mask_format  =  "polygons"  ,
)
```


For polygon output, the engine traces the default probability threshold of 0.50.5


0.5


using marching squares. Edge crossings are interpolated between neighbouring probabilities, then the contours are simplified. Coordinates are mapped back to the original image and expressed on axes from 0 to 1000.


The formats differ in what they retain.


Format Returned geometry


` largest` The largest exterior outline, the default


` polygons` Separate exterior outlines for disconnected pieces


` merged` Exterior pieces connected into one path by bridges


` bitmap` An uncompressed, column-major run-length encoding at the original image size


For the pole in the example,` polygons` keeps both exterior pieces.` largest` keeps just the larger one, while` merged` draws bridges to put them in a single path. Those bridges can cross background pixels. Polygon modes also omit hole boundaries, so choose` bitmap` when those interior gaps matter to your application.


For the bitmap, the engine bilinearly samples the probability field onto the original image, thresholds it and clips it to the box. The result contains` size` in height-width order and` counts` beginning with a background run. It is an RLE object, not an array of pixel rows. Thresholding and interpolation do not commute, so a rasterised polygon need not match this bitmap pixel for pixel.


## Where the name and score come from


The last step is attaching the contour to the object your app sees in the result. The language decoder supplies a name and attributes, along with a reference to a proposed region. That reference brings in the mask. Its coefficients were computed from image features at the box centre, independently of the words used to name it.


This places Mirage alongside several related approaches with different interfaces.[Segment Anything](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02643) accepts prompts such as points to select a mask.[CondInst](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.05664) predicts parameters for a small mask network for each instance. Here, we select a proposed object and combine shared image-dependent prototypes.


When you inspect the result, read the object's` score` as its detection-heatmap score. The name and contour need their own checks. A confident proposal can still have an inaccurate mask or the wrong name.


Supplying the correct boxes during evaluation helps isolate the mask head. Evaluating the whole system asks more of it, because the proposals must also be found, selected and named correctly. Keeping that distinction, the mask resolution and the output format visible makes results easier to interpret and reproduce.


If you'd like to see where this division of work comes from, the[structured perception article](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/structured-perception) explains the broader design.[OCR decoding](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/ocr-decoding) follows the same idea for text. Try the[Mirage playground](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/mirage#sandbox) with a thin object or two overlapping objects, and look at where the contour follows them and where it falls short. The same outputs are available through the[Cactus package](https://github.com/cactus-compute/cactus) .
